title: Array Data Structure and Random Access
content: An array is a contiguous block of memory locations, each storing an element of the same data type. Elements are accessed using a zero-based integer index, providing constant-time O(1) random access via memory offset calculation (base_address + index * element_size). Inserting or deleting an element at an arbitrary position requires shifting all subsequent elements, resulting in O(n) worst-case time complexity. Fixed-size arrays cannot expand beyond their allocated capacity.
summary: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory enabling O(1) index access with O(n) arbitrary insertion or deletion.
keywords: array, contiguous memory, indexing, random access, O(1), memory offset

title: Array Memory Layout and Spatial Cache Locality
content: Because arrays reside in sequential memory addresses, they demonstrate superior spatial cache locality compared to pointer-based structures. When an array element is loaded into CPU cache, adjacent elements are automatically fetched into the same cache line. This dramatically accelerates sequential iterations and linear scans. However, contiguous allocation requires finding a sufficiently large unfragmented memory segment during creation.
summary: Contiguous array memory layout maximizes CPU spatial cache locality for fast sequential processing.
keywords: cache locality, spatial locality, memory allocation, CPU cache line, sequential scan

title: Dynamic Arrays and Amortized Insertion Analysis
content: A dynamic array overcomes fixed capacity limitations by allocating a larger memory block when full (typically doubling capacity) and copying all n elements over. While the resizing step takes O(n) time, resizing occurs infrequently. Averaged over a sequence of n append operations, the aggregate work is O(n), yielding an amortized insertion time of O(1) per append at the end.
summary: Dynamic arrays resize by doubling capacity to achieve amortized O(1) append time complexity.
keywords: dynamic array, resizing, doubling strategy, amortized complexity, append

title: Singly Linked List Structure and Traversal
content: A singly linked list is a linear collection of node objects, where each node contains a data element and a reference (pointer) to the subsequent node. Linked lists do not require contiguous memory allocation. Accessing an element at index k requires traversing k pointers from the head node, taking O(n) time. In contrast, inserting or deleting a node at the head or immediately following a known node reference takes O(1) pointer updates.
summary: Linked lists consist of pointer-connected nodes; lookup takes O(n) while insertion given a pointer takes O(1).
keywords: linked list, singly linked list, node, pointer, head, traversal, O(1) insertion

title: Doubly and Circular Linked Lists
content: A doubly linked list node contains two pointer fields: next and prev, enabling bidirectional traversal. Deleting a given node is O(1) because the predecessor node is directly accessible without traversing from the head. In circular linked lists, the final node references the head node instead of null, facilitating round-robin scheduling. Doubly linked lists incur higher memory overhead due to storing two pointer references per node.
summary: Doubly linked lists store previous and next pointers for bidirectional traversal and O(1) node deletion.
keywords: doubly linked list, circular list, prev pointer, memory overhead, bidirectional traversal

title: Array vs Linked List Tradeoffs
content: The architectural tradeoff between arrays and linked lists centers on access patterns versus reallocation flexibility. Arrays provide O(1) random access and low memory overhead, but dynamic resizing requires O(n) reallocation and contiguous memory blocks. Linked lists allocate node memory dynamically on demand and allow O(1) insertion at known positions, but sacrifice random access, exhibit poor cache locality, and require extra memory for pointers.
summary: Arrays excel in random access and cache performance; linked lists excel in dynamic non-contiguous allocation.
keywords: comparison, trade-offs, memory overhead, random access, pointer overhead

title: Stack ADT and LIFO Discipline
content: A stack is a restricted linear data structure that operates under the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) discipline. Elements can only be added to or removed from one end, designated the top. The primary operations are push (add an element to the top) and pop (remove and return the top element), both executing in strict O(1) time complexity. Stacks also support a peek operation to inspect the top value without removing it.
summary: Stacks follow the Last-In First-Out (LIFO) rule with O(1) push, pop, and peek operations at the top.
keywords: stack, LIFO, push, pop, peek, top, constant time

title: Stack Implementations: Array vs Linked List
content: Stacks can be implemented using either dynamic arrays or singly linked lists. In an array-backed stack, the top is maintained by an integer index, taking O(1) operations until capacity is reached, which triggers an amortized resize. In a linked list stack, push prepends a new node at the head and pop removes the head node, guaranteeing strict O(1) worst-case time for every operation without resizing spikes, though with pointer memory overhead.
summary: Array stacks offer cache locality with amortized resizing; linked stacks offer strict O(1) operations without resizing.
keywords: stack implementation, array stack, linked stack, stack overflow, worst-case bound

title: Stack Applications: Call Stacks and Parsing
content: Stacks are fundamental across computer science. System execution environments use the call stack to store activation records containing return addresses and local variables during function calls. In compiler design, stacks are used for balanced parenthesis verification, expression evaluation, and conversion from infix to postfix (Reverse Polish) notation using Dijkstra's Shunting-yard algorithm.
summary: Stacks power function call execution, syntax checking, and arithmetic expression parsing.
keywords: call stack, activation record, parenthesis matching, postfix, shunting-yard

title: Queue ADT and FIFO Ordering
content: A queue is a linear collection governed by the First-In, First-Out (FIFO) ordering rule. Elements are inserted at the rear (enqueue) and removed from the front (dequeue). Both enqueue and dequeue execute in O(1) time complexity. Queues are essential in operating systems for CPU job scheduling, printer spooling, asynchronous messaging, and breadth-first graph traversals.
summary: Queues enforce First-In First-Out (FIFO) ordering with O(1) enqueue at rear and dequeue at front.
keywords: queue, FIFO, enqueue, dequeue, front, rear, scheduling, buffer

title: Circular Queue and Index Modulo Arithmetic
content: When implementing a queue with a fixed-size array, successive dequeue operations leave unused slots at the beginning. A circular queue resolves this by wrapping indices around using modulo arithmetic: index = (index + 1) % capacity. A circular queue maintains front and rear indices, preventing memory drift and enabling all operations to remain O(1) within bounded memory.
summary: Circular queues wrap array indices using modulo arithmetic to prevent space waste in fixed allocations.
keywords: circular queue, modulo arithmetic, index wrap, fixed capacity, ring buffer

title: Double-Ended Queue (Deque) and Priority Queue Differences
content: A double-ended queue (deque) generalizes stacks and queues by permitting O(1) insertion and deletion at both the front and rear. In contrast, a priority queue does not enforce FIFO ordering; instead, elements are dequeued according to an associated priority key, typically implemented via binary heaps with O(log n) insertion and removal.
summary: Deques allow O(1) access at both ends; priority queues order elements by key rather than arrival time.
keywords: deque, double-ended queue, priority queue, ordering, generalized queue

title: Recursion Principles and Base Cases
content: Recursion is an algorithmic problem-solving approach where a function invokes itself with smaller instances of the identical problem. Every valid recursive algorithm requires two components: at least one base case that terminates recursion without further self-calls, and a recursive step that shrinks input parameters strictly toward the base case. Omitting a base case causes infinite recursion and runtime stack overflow.
summary: Recursion requires terminating base cases and recursive steps that strictly reduce toward base cases.
keywords: recursion, base case, recursive step, termination, stack overflow, subproblem

title: Call Stack Mechanics and Activation Records
content: Each recursive call allocates a new activation record (stack frame) on the call stack to store parameters, local variables, and return instruction pointers. The maximum recursion depth determines the auxiliary memory complexity, typically O(depth). Deep recursive chains risk exceeding call stack limits, provoking StackOverflowError.
summary: Recursive calls allocate stack frames, creating auxiliary memory proportional to recursion depth.
keywords: call stack, activation record, stack frame, recursion depth, memory footprint

title: Recursive Data Structures and Tree Processing
content: A recursive data structure is defined in terms of smaller instances of itself. A binary tree is inherently recursive: it is either empty, or consists of a root node referencing two independent binary trees (left and right subtrees). Recursive algorithms on recursive structures naturally partition computation into subproblems matching the structure's inductive definition.
summary: Recursive data structures like trees are inductively defined and naturally processed via recursive algorithms.
keywords: recursive data structure, structural recursion, binary tree, inductive definition

title: Tree Data Structure Hierarchy and Properties
content: A tree is a non-linear hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes linked by directed edges without cycles. The unique starting node is the root; nodes without children are leaves. A key mathematical property is that any connected tree with n vertices contains exactly n - 1 edges. The depth of a node is the edge count from root to node, and tree height is the length of the longest path from root to a leaf.
summary: Trees are hierarchical acyclic structures where an n-node tree contains exactly n - 1 edges.
keywords: tree, root, leaf, parent, child, height, depth, edges, hierarchical

title: Tree Traversals: Preorder Inorder and Postorder
content: Depth-first tree traversals systematically visit all n nodes in O(n) time. Preorder traversal processes the current node first, followed by left and right subtrees (Node, Left, Right), useful for cloning tree structures. Inorder traversal processes Left, Node, Right, which produces sorted keys in binary search trees. Postorder processes Left, Right, Node, which is required for bottom-up operations like tree deletion.
summary: Preorder (N-L-R), Inorder (L-N-R), and Postorder (L-R-N) traversals visit all tree nodes in O(n) time.
keywords: tree traversal, preorder, inorder, postorder, depth-first traversal

title: The Full Binary Tree Theorem and Leaf Invariants
content: The Full Binary Tree Theorem states that the number of leaf nodes in a non-empty full binary tree is always one more than the number of internal nodes: L = I + 1. Furthermore, any full binary tree with n internal nodes contains exactly 2n + 1 total nodes and n + 1 empty pointer references (null branches). This theorem provides exact space lower bounds for tree pointer overhead.
summary: In a full binary tree, leaf count equals internal node count plus one (L = I + 1).
keywords: full binary tree theorem, internal nodes, leaf nodes, null pointers, space bounds

title: Binary Search Tree Property and Invariant
content: A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree where every node satisfies the global BST invariant: all keys in the node's entire left subtree are strictly less than the node's key, and all keys in the node's entire right subtree are strictly greater than the node's key. This property must hold across all descendants, not merely immediate children. An inorder traversal of a valid BST always yields keys in monotonically ascending sorted order.
summary: BST invariant requires all left subtree keys < node < all right subtree keys; inorder traversal yields sorted output.
keywords: binary search tree, BST, invariant, subtree ordering, inorder sorted, key comparison

title: BST Operations: Search Insertion and Deletion
content: Searching, inserting, and deleting keys in a BST follow comparison branching: compare with current node and branch left or right. The time complexity of these operations is proportional to tree height: O(h). In a balanced BST with n nodes, height h = O(log n). Deleting a node with two children requires replacing it with its inorder predecessor (maximum of left subtree) or inorder successor (minimum of right subtree).
summary: BST operations depend on tree height h: O(log n) when balanced, requiring predecessor/successor swaps for deletion.
keywords: BST search, BST insertion, BST deletion, inorder successor, tree height, O(h)

title: Degenerate Skewed BSTs and Information Flow
content: Validating whether an arbitrary binary tree is a valid BST requires checking global subtree bounds, not just parent-child pairs. When elements are inserted into a standard BST in pre-sorted order, the tree degenerates into a linear chain of height h = n, degrading search and insertion to O(n) worst-case time. Balancing mechanisms enforce logarithmic height bounds by restructuring nodes during mutations.
summary: Validating BSTs requires global subtree bounds; unbalanced insertions degrade performance to linear O(n).
keywords: BST validation, information flow, skewed tree, degenerate BST, worst case O(n)

title: Binary Heap Properties and Priority Queues
content: A binary heap is a complete binary tree that maintains the heap-order property. In a max-heap, every parent node is greater than or equal to its children, ensuring the maximum key resides at the root. In a min-heap, the root holds the minimum key. Because heaps are complete binary trees, they are stored compactly in contiguous arrays without pointer overhead, serving as the standard implementation for priority queues.
summary: Binary heaps are complete binary trees enforcing min/max heap property, efficiently stored in arrays.
keywords: heap, min-heap, max-heap, complete binary tree, priority queue, heap property

title: Array Representation for Complete Binary Trees
content: In an array-backed heap of size n, for a node at index i, its left child is at 2i + 1, right child at 2i + 2, and parent at (i - 1) // 2. Inserting an element appends it to the array end and sifts up (bubbles up) by swapping with smaller parents in O(log n) time. Extracting the root swaps it with the last element, decrements size, and sifts down in O(log n) time.
summary: Heap array indices link parents and children; insertion and extraction maintain invariants in O(log n) time.
keywords: heap array representation, sift up, sift down, bubble up, extract root, O(log n)

title: Linear Time Heap Construction: Bottom-Up Heapify
content: Building a heap from an arbitrary array of n items by repeated insertions takes O(n log n) time. However, bottom-up heapify builds a valid heap in linear O(n) time. It processes nodes backwards from the last non-leaf node (index n//2 - 1) down to the root, applying sift-down at each node. Because lower nodes have smaller heights and the majority of nodes reside near the bottom, the total swap bound sums to O(n).
summary: Bottom-up heapify builds a complete heap from an array in O(n) linear time rather than O(n log n).
keywords: heapify, build heap, bottom-up, linear time O(n), summation bound

title: Comparison Sorting Overview and Theoretical Lower Bound
content: Comparison-based sorting algorithms determine element order solely by pairwise comparisons. Elementary algorithms like Bubble Sort and Selection Sort take O(n^2) time. Advanced divide-and-conquer algorithms like Merge Sort and Quicksort achieve O(n log n) average time. Information theory dictates a strict mathematical lower bound: any comparison sort requires Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, proven via decision tree height log(n!).
summary: Comparison sorts have an Omega(n log n) theoretical lower bound based on decision tree height log(n!).
keywords: sorting, comparison sort, lower bound, Omega(n log n), decision tree, bubble sort

title: Quicksort vs Merge Sort Algorithmic Tradeoffs
content: Merge Sort divides an array into halves, sorts recursively, and merges sorted sub-arrays. It guarantees O(n log n) time in all cases and is stable, but requires O(n) auxiliary space. Quicksort partitions in-place around a pivot with O(log n) stack space and O(n log n) average time, but its worst case degrades to O(n^2) if extreme pivots are repeatedly chosen. Randomized pivoting avoids this worst-case degradation in practice.
summary: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) stability with O(n) space; Quicksort is in-place with O(n^2) worst case.
keywords: quicksort, merge sort, pivot, partition, stability, in-place sort, worst-case O(n^2)

title: Insertion Sort and Adaptive Behavior on Nearly-Sorted Data
content: Insertion Sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by inserting each item into its correct position among previously sorted elements. Although its worst-case is O(n^2) for reverse-sorted inputs, Insertion Sort is adaptive: on inputs with few inversions (nearly sorted), it executes in linear O(n) time with O(1) auxiliary space. For this reason, hybrid sorting algorithms (like Timsort) switch to Insertion Sort for small sub-arrays.
summary: Insertion Sort is adaptive, running in O(n) time on nearly sorted data with O(1) auxiliary space.
keywords: insertion sort, adaptive sort, inversions, nearly sorted, O(n) best case, timsort

title: Hash Table Foundations and Hash Functions
content: A hash table implements an associative dictionary mapping keys to values. A hash function converts an arbitrary key into an integer index within an array of buckets. When hash keys are uniformly distributed and the load factor (alpha = n / m) is bounded, insertion, deletion, and lookup execute in expected O(1) average time. However, if keys collide into the same bucket, lookup performance degrades to O(n) worst-case time.
summary: Hash tables map keys to bucket indices for average O(1) operations, degrading to O(n) under severe collisions.
keywords: hash table, hash function, bucket, load factor, expected O(1), worst-case O(n)

title: Collision Resolution via Separate Chaining
content: A hash collision occurs when two distinct keys yield identical hash indices. In separate chaining (open hashing), each bucket in the table maintains a linked list of collided key-value pairs. Inserting a new key prepends it to the bucket list in O(1) time. Searching requires traversing the bucket list, which takes O(1 + alpha) average time. Separate chaining handles load factors greater than 1.0 gracefully without table saturation.
summary: Separate chaining stores collided entries in bucket linked lists, handling load factors gracefully.
keywords: collisions, separate chaining, linked buckets, load factor alpha, collision resolution

title: Collision Resolution via Open Addressing and Probing
content: In open addressing, all key-value entries are stored directly in the bucket array itself without auxiliary lists. When a collision occurs, alternative slots are checked according to a probe sequence. Linear probing checks successive slots (index + i) % m, which is susceptible to primary clustering. Quadratic probing and double hashing mitigate clustering by varying probe step sizes. Open addressing strictly requires load factor alpha < 1.0.
summary: Open addressing stores entries directly in buckets using probe sequences, requiring load factor < 1.0.
keywords: open addressing, linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing, primary clustering

title: Graph Representation: Adjacency Matrix vs Adjacency List
content: A graph G = (V, E) comprises vertices V and edges E. An adjacency matrix is a |V| x |V| boolean or weight matrix enabling O(1) edge existence queries, but requires O(|V|^2) space and O(|V|) time to find neighbors, making it inefficient for sparse graphs. An adjacency list represents each vertex with a list of its adjacent edges, consuming O(|V| + |E|) space. Adjacency lists are optimal for sparse graphs where |E| << |V|^2.
summary: Adjacency lists use O(|V|+|E|) space optimal for sparse graphs; adjacency matrices use O(|V|^2) space.
keywords: graph, vertex, edge, adjacency list, adjacency matrix, sparse graph, dense graph

title: Graph Connectivity and Connected Components
content: An undirected graph is connected if a path exists between every pair of vertices. Disconnected graphs are partitioned into connected components: maximal subgraphs in which all vertices are mutually reachable. In directed graphs, a strongly connected component (SCC) requires bidirectional reachability between every vertex pair. Connected components can be identified in O(|V| + |E|) time by launching graph traversals from unvisited vertices.
summary: Connected components partition graphs into mutually reachable subgraphs, computable in O(|V|+|E|) time.
keywords: connectivity, connected components, strongly connected, SCC, reachability

title: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) and Topological Sorting
content: A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a directed graph containing no directed cycles. Topological sorting produces a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge u -> v, vertex u precedes v in the sequence. Topological sorting is only possible for DAGs and can be computed in O(|V| + |E|) time using Kahn's in-degree algorithm (FIFO queue) or via reverse postorder of Depth-First Search.
summary: Topological sort orders DAG vertices linearly such that dependencies precede targets in O(|V|+|E|) time.
keywords: DAG, directed acyclic graph, topological sort, Kahn algorithm, dependencies

title: Breadth-First Search Mechanics and FIFO Queue
content: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores a graph level by level, visiting all vertices at distance k before proceeding to vertices at distance k + 1. BFS utilizes a FIFO queue to sequence vertex visits and maintains a boolean visited set to avoid cycles. The total time complexity is O(|V| + |E|) when using an adjacency list, with O(|V|) auxiliary queue space.
summary: BFS traverses graphs level by level using a FIFO queue and visited set in O(|V| + |E|) time.
keywords: BFS, breadth-first search, FIFO queue, visited set, level-order, graph exploration

title: BFS Shortest Path Guarantee in Unweighted Graphs
content: In any unweighted graph (or graph where all edge weights are equal), Breadth-First Search is mathematically guaranteed to find the shortest path (minimum edge count) from a designated start vertex to all reachable vertices. Because BFS explores edges in increasing order of path length, the first time a vertex is dequeued, its minimum distance is permanently established. BFS cannot compute shortest paths on weighted graphs.
summary: BFS guarantees finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs because it explores edges in ascending distance order.
keywords: BFS shortest path, unweighted graph, edge distance, minimum path, queue

title: BFS Applications: Bipartite Graph Verification
content: BFS is widely utilized to test whether an undirected graph is bipartite (2-colorable). Starting from an uncolored vertex, BFS assigns alternating colors (e.g. red and blue) to adjacent levels. If an edge is discovered connecting two vertices assigned the identical color, the graph contains an odd-length cycle and is not bipartite. This verification executes in O(|V| + |E|) time.
summary: BFS tests bipartite graphs in O(|V|+|E|) time by checking for color conflicts between adjacent levels.
keywords: bipartite, 2-colorable, graph coloring, odd cycle, level alternating

title: Depth-First Search Mechanics and Backtracking
content: Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking. It can be implemented recursively using the system call stack or iteratively using an explicit LIFO stack along with a visited set. In an adjacency list representation, DFS runs in O(|V| + |E|) time and consumes O(|V|) auxiliary space for the stack and visited array.
summary: DFS explores deeply along paths before backtracking, utilizing a LIFO call stack in O(|V| + |E|) time.
keywords: DFS, depth-first search, LIFO stack, backtracking, visited array, recursion

title: DFS Edge Classification and Invariants
content: During DFS traversal of a graph, edges are categorized into four types: tree edges (discovering unvisited vertices), back edges (connecting a vertex to an ancestor in the DFS tree), forward edges (connecting to a descendant), and cross edges (connecting unrelated subtrees). In undirected graphs, only tree edges and back edges exist. A graph contains a cycle if and only if a back edge is encountered.
summary: DFS classifies edges into tree, back, forward, and cross edges; back edges definitively indicate cycles.
keywords: edge classification, tree edge, back edge, forward edge, cross edge, cycle detection

title: Cycle Detection in Directed Graphs via DFS Recursion Stack
content: Cycle detection in directed graphs requires distinguishing vertices currently in the active recursion call stack from vertices already fully explored. Vertices are tracked with a 3-state system: unvisited, currently visiting (on recursion stack), and completely visited. If DFS encounters an edge leading to a vertex marked as currently visiting, a directed cycle (back edge) is confirmed. This executes in O(|V| + |E|) time.
summary: Directed cycle detection tracks active recursion stack nodes using a 3-state visited system in O(|V|+|E|) time.
keywords: cycle detection, directed graph, recursion stack, 3-state visited, back edge
